title: Liaison — Linking Sounds (연음)
plainEnglish: When a syllable ends in a consonant and the next starts with ㅇ (a vowel), that consonant slides over to begin the next syllable.
whenToUse: Reach for this rule every single time a written 받침 is followed by a syllable that begins with ㅇ — which in practice means almost every particle and ending you attach to a noun or verb stem. The moment you add 이/은/을/에 to a noun that ends in a consonant, the consonant relocates: 책 + 을 is heard 채글, 집 + 에 is heard 지베, 밥 + 을 is heard 바블. It is also why a verb stem links into its ending — 먹 + 어요 → [머거요], 읽 + 으면 → [일그면]. The term 연음 literally means 連音 'connect-sound', and that is exactly the intent: Korean refuses to leave a vowel-initial syllable 'naked', so it borrows the consonant next door. Whenever your ear can't match a textbook word to what you heard, suspect liaison first.
attachmentRule: A final consonant (받침) before an ㅇ-initial syllable moves to become that syllable's onset: 꽃 + 이 → [꼬치], 음악 + 을 → [으마글], 옷 + 이 → [오시], 한국 + 어 → [한구거]. A double 받침 splits — the left one stays as the 받침, the right one moves: 읽 + 어 → [일거], 앉 + 아 → [안자], 없 + 어요 → [업서요]. Liaison does not cross a clear pause between separate words, and ㅎ-받침 is the exception that drops instead of linking (좋아요 → [조아요], not [조하요]).
contrastWith: Do not confuse 연음 (liaison) with 비음화 (nasalization): both keep the spelling fixed, but they are triggered by opposite neighbours. Liaison fires before a VOWEL (the silent ㅇ) and simply slides the consonant over unchanged — 국이 → [구기], the ㄱ survives. Nasalization fires before ㄴ/ㅁ and CHANGES the consonant — 국물 → [궁물], the ㄱ becomes ㅇ. Same word 국, totally different outcome depending on whether 이 or 물 follows. So your first check is always: is the next syllable a bare vowel, or a nasal? And remember you still WRITE 꽃이, 음악을, 한국어 either way — only the pronunciation links.

examples.en: The flowers are really pretty. (sounds like 꼬치)
I listen to music. (sounds like 으마글)
The clothes are too small. (sounds like 오시)

commonMistakes: Pronouncing each block separately — saying 꼳·이 instead of 꼬치. English keeps word edges crisp, so learners 'reset' at every block. Why it's wrong: Korean treats 받침 + 이 as one flow, so the careful version sounds robotic. Fix: let the final consonant become the next syllable's first sound — say 꼬·치, 으·마글, 오·시.

Forgetting that a double 받침 splits, e.g. saying [익어요] for 읽어요. Why it's wrong: only ONE consonant of ㄺ can move; the ㄹ stays put and the ㄱ slides over, giving [일거요]. Fix: keep the left letter as the 받침 and move the right letter — 읽어요 → [일거요], 앉아 → [안자].
Trying to link ㅎ-받침 like any other consonant, e.g. saying [조하요] for 좋아요. Why it's wrong: ㅎ before a vowel disappears rather than sliding over. Fix: drop the ㅎ entirely — 좋아요 → [조아요], 많아요 → [마나요].
studyOrder: Spot a 받침 followed by ㅇ
Slide the 받침 into the next syllable
For double 받침, keep one and move one
beginnerExplanation: Mnemonic: think of the silent ㅇ as an empty chair, and the 받침 next door as someone who can't stand an empty seat — it slides over to fill it. Korean is written in neat syllable blocks, but in speech a final consonant 'jumps' onto the next block whenever that block starts with a vowel (the silent ㅇ). So 한국어 is read 한구거, and 꽃이 is read 꼬치. You keep spelling it the normal way — only the sound links up. Two warnings live with this rule: a double 받침 only lends ONE consonant (읽어요 → 일거요), and ㅎ ducks out instead of jumping (좋아요 → 조아요). Once you expect this slide, listening gets dramatically easier.

title: Nasalization (비음화)
plainEnglish: A stop consonant (ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ) turns into a nasal (ㅇ/ㄴ/ㅁ) when the next syllable starts with ㄴ or ㅁ.
whenToUse: This is the rule that makes the most common phrase you'll ever say — 감사합니다 → [감사함니다] — and the entire polite -습니다/-ㅂ니다 ending sound the way natives say it, never the way it's spelled. Apply it any time a ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ-type 받침 bumps directly into ㄴ or ㅁ: 학년 → [항년], 국물 → [궁물], 받는 → [반는], 입니다 → [임니다]. The Korean tongue physically resists going from a hard closed stop straight into a nasal, so it 'pre-nasalizes' the stop to match. Because 비음화 (鼻音化, 'nose-sound-change') is automatic and exceptionless in these contexts, you can't opt out: even slow, careful speech does it. Train your ear on it early, because -ㅂ니다 endings are everywhere in formal Korean.
attachmentRule: Before ㄴ or ㅁ: a ㄱ-type 받침 (ㄱㄲㅋㄳㄺ) → ㅇ (학년 → [항년], 국물 → [궁물], 깎는 → [깡는]); a ㄷ-type 받침 (ㄷㅅㅆㅈㅊㅌㅎ) → ㄴ (받는 → [반는], 옛날 → [옌날], 꽃만 → [꼰만]); a ㅂ-type 받침 (ㅂㅍㄼㄿ) → ㅁ (입니다 → [임니다], 앞문 → [암문], 밟는 → [밤는]). The trigger consonant ㄴ/ㅁ itself never changes — only the 받침 in front of it does.
contrastWith: Contrast 비음화 with 격음화 (aspiration), because both involve stops but do opposite things. Nasalization SOFTENS a stop into a nasal when ㄴ/ㅁ follows — 국물 → [궁물], the ㄱ goes airy and nasal. Aspiration HARDENS sounds into a breathy stop when ㅎ is involved — 좋다 → [조타], the sound gets sharper, not softer. So the neighbour decides everything: ㄴ/ㅁ → go nasal; ㅎ → go aspirated. Also keep it apart from liaison, which needs a bare vowel: 학년 nasalizes to [항년], but 학원 (with vowel ㅝ) just links to [하권]. The spelling, of course, stays 입니다, 학년 in every case.

examples.en: I'm in third grade. (학년 sounds like 항년)
The broth is hot. (국물 sounds like 궁물)
This is Korean food. (입니다 sounds like 임니다)

commonMistakes: Pronouncing 합니다 exactly as written, with a hard ㅂ, instead of [함니다]. Why it's wrong: a ㅂ 받침 in front of ㄴ must become ㅁ, so the careful spelling-pronunciation sounds foreign and stiff. Fix: route every -ㅂ니다 ending through ㅁ — 합니다 → [함니다], 갑니다 → [감니다].

Missing nasalization in the -습니다 ending and saying [-습니다] crisply. Why it's wrong: the ㅂ before ㄴ nasalizes, so it is always [-슴니다] in real speech (감사합니다 → 감사함니다). Fix: bake [-슴니다] / [-ㅁ니다] into your default for all formal endings.

Applying it across a real pause or to the wrong direction, e.g. nasalizing the ㄴ/ㅁ itself. Why it's wrong: only the STOP 받침 (ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ) changes; ㄴ and ㅁ are the triggers and stay exactly as they are. Fix: change just the 받침 in front — 국물 → [궁물], leaving 물 untouched.
studyOrder: Find a ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ 받침 before ㄴ or ㅁ
beginnerExplanation: Analogy: a hard stop 받침 standing next to ㄴ/ㅁ is like someone catching a yawn from the person beside them — the nasal 'spreads', and the stop goes nasal to match. A ㄱ-sound becomes ㅇ (학년 → 항년), a ㄷ-sound becomes ㄴ (받는 → 반는), and a ㅂ-sound becomes ㅁ (입니다 → 임니다). Mnemonic for the pairs: each stop moves to the nasal made in the same place in your mouth — ㄱ and ㅇ are both in the throat, ㄷ and ㄴ both at the ridge behind your teeth, ㅂ and ㅁ both at the lips. That's why the polite -습니다 ending is pronounced -슴니다, and 감사합니다 comes out 감사함니다. You never change the spelling — just let the sound go through your nose.

title: Palatalization (구개음화)
plainEnglish: A final ㄷ or ㅌ turns into ㅈ or ㅊ when the next sound is 이 (or 히).
whenToUse: Use this whenever a syllable ending in ㄷ or ㅌ is followed by 이 or 히 — most importantly in the everyday word 같이 → [가치] ('together'), plus 굳이 → [구지] ('needlessly'), 끝이 → [끄치] ('the end'), and verbs like 붙이다 → [부치다] ('to stick on'). The intent behind 구개음화 (口蓋音化, literally 'palate-sound-change') is that the vowel 이 is made up near the hard palate, so a tongue-tip ㄷ/ㅌ gets dragged forward to that same spot and lands as ㅈ/ㅊ. Crucially this only happens across a meaningful boundary — a 받침 meeting a particle or a suffix 이/히 — not inside a single root, which is why 잔디 ('grass') stays plainly [잔디]. In day-to-day speech you'll meet it most in 같이, so make that one automatic.
attachmentRule: When a 받침 ㄷ/ㅌ meets the vowel 이: ㄷ + 이 → 지 (굳이 → [구지], 해돋이 → [해도지], 맏이 → [마지]); ㅌ + 이 → 치 (같이 → [가치], 끝이 → [끄치], 붙이다 → [부치다]). With 히 it also applies because ㅌ+ㅎ first aspirate and then palatalize: 닫히다 → [다치다], 묻히다 → [무치다]. It does NOT apply when ㄷ/ㅌ and 이 sit inside one morpheme (잔디 → [잔디], 느티나무 → [느티나무]).
contrastWith: Frame 구개음화 as a special, 'extra-step' cousin of plain 연음 (liaison). With an ordinary 받침, liaison just slides the consonant over unchanged: 굳이 by liaison alone would be [구디]. But because the following vowel is specifically 이, the sound takes one further step forward in the mouth and becomes [구지]. So the dividing line is the vowel and the consonant: ONLY ㄷ/ㅌ, and ONLY before 이/히, get this upgrade — 밭이 → [바치], but 밭을 (vowel ㅡ) merely links to [바틀]. Same 받침 ㅌ, two different results depending on whether 이 or 을 follows.

examples.en: Shall we go together? (같이 sounds like 가치)
You don't have to come (no need). (굳이 sounds like 구지)
I can't see the end. (끝이 sounds like 끄치)
I'm going to see the sunrise. (해돋이 sounds like 해도지)

commonMistakes: Reading 같이 letter-by-letter as [가티]. Why it's wrong: before 이 the ㅌ shifts forward to ㅊ, so the literal version is not how anyone says this very common word. Fix: lock in 같이 → [가치], and by the same logic 굳이 → [구지].

Over-applying the rule to consonants or vowels it doesn't cover, e.g. trying to palatalize 받을 → [바줄]. Why it's wrong: only ㄷ/ㅌ before 이/히 qualify; before 을 (vowel ㅡ) you get plain liaison [바들]. Fix: check both conditions — is the 받침 ㄷ/ㅌ AND is the next vowel 이/히? If not, just link normally.

Forcing it inside a single root word, e.g. saying 잔디 as [잔지]. Why it's wrong: palatalization needs a boundary between a stem and a suffix/particle; within one morpheme like 잔디 nothing changes. Fix: keep root-internal ㄷ/ㅌ plain — 잔디 → [잔디], 느티나무 → [느티나무].
studyOrder: Spot a ㄷ or ㅌ 받침 right before 이/히
Remember the common word 같이 → 가치
beginnerExplanation: Mnemonic: the vowel 이 lives high up near the roof of your mouth (the palate), and it 'pulls' a tongue-tip ㄷ/ㅌ up to meet it, where they soften into ㅈ/ㅊ. So 같이 ('together') is said 가치, and 굳이 is 구지. Two guardrails keep you from overusing it: it fires only before 이 or 히 (not other vowels — 밭을 stays [바틀]), and only across a stem-plus-suffix seam (so the single word 잔디 stays [잔디]). It's a small rule, but 같이 is such an everyday word that getting it right (가치, not 가티) instantly makes you sound more natural.

title: Aspiration (격음화)
plainEnglish: ㅎ merges with a neighboring ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ/ㅈ to make the strong, breathy ㅋ/ㅌ/ㅍ/ㅊ.
whenToUse: Use this whenever ㅎ touches ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ/ㅈ in either order — it powers warm, high-frequency words like 축하해요 → [추카해요] ('congratulations'), 좋다 → [조타] ('it's good'), 못해요 → [모태요] ('I can't'), and 입학 → [이팍] ('entering school'). The breath of ㅎ doesn't disappear and doesn't stay separate; it fuses into the neighbouring stop to create one strong puff of air. 격음화 (激音化, 'fierce-sound-change') captures the feel exactly: the result is a single forceful, aspirated consonant. Because this is automatic, you should produce it even in careful speech — saying the two letters apart sounds distinctly non-native. Watch especially for ㅎ-final stems before an ending (좋다, 좋지, 많다) and for ㅅ-type 받침 meeting 해 (못해 → [모태]).
attachmentRule: ㅎ + ㄱ (or ㄱ + ㅎ) → ㅋ: 축하 → [추카], 그렇게 → [그러케]. ㅎ + ㄷ → ㅌ: 좋다 → [조타], 많다 → [만타]. ㅎ + ㅂ → ㅍ: 입학 → [이팍], 잡히다 → [자피다]. ㅎ + ㅈ → ㅊ: 좋지 → [조치], 맞히다 → [마치다]. A ㅅ/ㄷ-type 받침 (which sounds like [ㄷ]) before 해 also aspirates: 못해 → [모태], 깨끗하다 → [깨끄타다].
contrastWith: Set 격음화 against 비음화 (nasalization), since both reshape stops but in opposite directions. Aspiration HARDENS: a stop plus ㅎ fuses into a sharp, breathy ㅋ/ㅌ/ㅍ/ㅊ — 좋다 → [조타], more air, more force. Nasalization SOFTENS: a stop before ㄴ/ㅁ goes airy and nasal — 좋네 → [존네], the sound relaxes into the nose. So the neighbour is the giveaway: ㅎ → aspirate (harder); ㄴ/ㅁ → nasalize (softer). Also separate it from liaison: ㅎ never simply 'links' to a following vowel — 좋아요 drops the ㅎ to [조아요], but 좋다 fuses it into [조타]. The two plain sounds become ONE aspirated sound; you do not hear ㅎ on its own.

examples.en: The weather is really nice. (좋다 sounds like 조타)
I can't do that. (못해 sounds like 모태)
I entered university. (입학 sounds like 이팍)

commonMistakes: Trying to pronounce ㅎ as a separate sound, e.g. saying [조ㅎ다] for 좋다. Why it's wrong: ㅎ and the stop fuse into one aspirated consonant, so an audible separate ㅎ breaks the word. Fix: collapse them into a single strong sound — 좋다 → [조타], 많다 → [만타].

Missing aspiration in 못해 / 깨끗하다 and saying them flatly. Why it's wrong: the [ㄷ]-sounding 받침 plus 해 must aspirate to ㅌ, giving [모태] / [깨끄타다]; the plain version sounds off. Fix: treat 받침 + 해 as a trigger — 못해 → [모태].

Confusing it with the ㅎ-drop of liaison, e.g. carrying the logic of 좋아요 → [조아요] over to 좋다. Why it's wrong: before a VOWEL ㅎ disappears, but before a STOP it fuses and aspirates — different outcomes. Fix: vowel after ㅎ → drop it (좋아요 → 조아요); stop after ㅎ → fuse it (좋다 → 조타).
studyOrder: Find a ㅎ next to ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ/ㅈ (either order)
Practice 좋다 → 조타 and 축하 → 추카
beginnerExplanation: Mnemonic: the letter ㅎ is a puff of breath, and when it bumps into ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ, or ㅈ, that breath gets 'baked into' the consonant — two letters melt into one strong, breathy sound: ㅋ, ㅌ, ㅍ, ㅊ. So 좋다 is said 조타, 축하 is 추카, 못해 is 모태, and 입학 is 이팍. Order doesn't matter — ㅎ before or after the stop gives the same fusion. One thing to keep straight: ㅎ only fuses with a stop; when a plain vowel follows instead, the ㅎ quietly drops (좋아요 → 조아요). You won't hear the ㅎ on its own either way — it's absorbed into the harder sound.
